deep.reconstruction:
This is a private memorandum page, not mathematics. It has three practical records and a stray number.

(A) 'Briefpapiergewicht 1847 Febr 20' (letter-paper weight). Gauss records, for several kinds of writing paper, how many sheets (Bogen) make one pound (℔):
1) Ribbed Dutch paper (gerippt holländisch), bought 19 Feb 1847: 88.2 sheets per lb.
2) 'GR Superfine': 105.8 sheets per lb.
3) Bath paper: 104.2 sheets per lb.
4) Older paper, of which he had much ('Aelteres wovon viel'): A. fine, 93.9 sheets per lb; B. coarse, 64.0 sheets per lb.
5) Fine writing paper: 55.1 sheets per lb.

The decimal values suggest he weighed a counted stack and divided; the raw data are not recorded. In modern terms the weight of one sheet is w = P/n, where P is one local pound and n the sheets per pound. In Loth (32 Loth = 1 lb), paper 1 gives 32/88.2 ≈ 0.363 Loth per sheet. Paper 2 gives ≈ 0.302 Loth, and paper 5 gives ≈ 0.581 Loth. Taking a pound of roughly 467–490 g (the exact Hanoverian pound in 1847 is not certain here), a sheet weighs roughly 4.4–8.9 g. The obvious purpose, my inference, is estimating letter weight for postage, which was charged by Loth.

(B) 'Ausgeloosete Stieglitze Junius 1847': serial numbers of series drawn for redemption in June 1847, for the Russian government loans handled by the bank Stieglitz & Co. These are copied from a published drawing list to check his own holdings.
- 2nd loan: 79, 92, 98, 107, 285, 297, 315, 316 (8 series).
- 3rd loan: 7, 45, 118, 128, 159, 222, 230, 319 (8 series).
- 4th loan: 113, 131, 174, 176, 209, 233, 234, 292, 313, 370, 392, 447 (12 series).
The next page continues the same practice for Norwegian bonds in 1849–50.

(C) 'Coupons wiegen' (coupons weigh): 1575 Austrian coupons make 1 lb, and 470.4 Hanoverian coupons make 1 lb. So one Austrian coupon weighs 1/1575 lb (≈0.0203 Loth) and one Hanoverian coupon 1/470.4 lb (≈0.068 Loth). A Hanoverian coupon is about 3.35 times as heavy as an Austrian one. The likely use, my inference, is counting or valuing coupons by weight, or estimating postage for mailing them.

(D) 'P. 16856.' is an isolated number, possibly a package, receipt or account number. Its meaning cannot be determined from the page.
errors: No mathematical errors are possible to detect. The figures are empirical measurements with no shown derivation. The lists are internally consistent: each is in increasing order with no duplicates.
